title: What a Commercial Door Baseline Survey Covers (and Why FMs Use It)
description: A baseline survey documents every bay door, gate, and dock leveler on a property before anything breaks. What it covers, and why facilities managers use it for budgeting.

h1: What a Commercial Door Baseline Survey Covers (and Why FMs Use It for Budgeting)
intro: Ask a facilities manager how many overhead doors are on their property and you'll usually get a confident number. Ask what age they are, what springs are in them, and which ones are closest to failing, and the confidence drops fast. A baseline survey is how you close that gap — a single walkthrough that turns "we have some doors" into a door-by-door record you can actually plan a budget around. Here's what's actually in one, and why it earns its place ahead of any maintenance contract.

sections.heading: What a baseline survey actually is
sections.body:
It's a documented, door-by-door inspection of every overhead door, rolling gate, and piece of dock equipment on a property — done once, up front, before any ongoing maintenance schedule starts. A technician walks the site and records, for each opening: door type and size, approximate age, spring type and condition, operator make and condition, estimated daily cycle count, and any damage or wear already visible.

The output isn't a verbal "things look okay." It's a written per-door record — the kind of document that survives staff turnover, gets handed to a new property manager, and sits next to the budget spreadsheet instead of living in one technician's memory. If your current maintenance history is a stack of invoices for whichever door happened to break, a baseline survey is the thing that was always supposed to come before that stack started.

sections.heading: Why you can't maintain what you haven't counted
sections.body:
Most multi-door properties didn't acquire their doors all at once. A warehouse adds a bay here, swaps an opener there, and twenty years later nobody on staff remembers which door got new springs in 2019 and which one still has the originals. That's not a knock on facilities staff — it's just what happens when equipment turns over slower than the people managing it.

The practical cost shows up at budget time. Without a baseline, every door repair is a surprise line item, and every capital request for door replacement is a guess dressed up as a number. With one, you know which three doors are carrying the most daily cycles, which springs are past their rated life, and which operator is the oldest thing on the property — which means the budget request is backed by a document instead of a hunch.

sections.heading: What gets documented on each door
sections.body:
A thorough survey records the same fields for every opening, so doors can be compared against each other instead of evaluated one at a time in isolation:

- **Door type and dimensions** — sectional steel, rolling steel curtain, or a dock door with integrated leveler, plus width and height for future parts ordering
- **Spring type, size, and condition** — torsion or barrel spring, visible rust or gaps, and whether it's a standard-cycle or high-cycle unit
- **Estimated daily cycle count** — how many times the door actually opens and closes in a working day, which drives how fast every component wears
- **Operator condition** — make, apparent age, drive type (chain, belt, or direct), and whether force and limit settings look correctly adjusted
- **Track, roller, and hardware condition** — alignment, rust, dents from forklift or cart strikes
- **Safety devices** — photo eyes and sensing edges present and functioning
- **Dock-specific equipment** — leveler hinges and springs, dock seals and shelters, where applicable
- **Visible damage or deferred repairs** — anything already broken or compromised, flagged separately from normal wear

That list overlaps with what a routine maintenance visit checks — see our [commercial maintenance schedule by door type](/blog/commercial-garage-door-maintenance-schedule-by-door-type/) for how those checks differ between sectional doors, rolling steel gates, and dock equipment. The difference with a baseline survey is timing and purpose: it happens once, up front, to build the record every later maintenance visit gets compared against.

sections.heading: How facilities managers use it for budgeting
sections.body:
A baseline survey turns three kinds of budget decisions from guesswork into documentation:

**Prioritizing capital requests.** If a baseline shows one dock door running 40+ cycles a day on a spring rated for a fraction of that load, it's the obvious candidate for a high-cycle spring upgrade before it fails mid-shift — and that's a specific, defensible line in next year's capital plan rather than a generic "doors need attention" request.

**Scoping a maintenance contract that fits the actual fleet.** A property with twelve doors in a mix of ages and duty cycles doesn't need (or benefit from) one flat quarterly visit applied identically to all twelve. A baseline is what lets a maintenance program get scoped by door, with busier and older doors checked more often than a low-traffic side door — our [commercial maintenance contracts](/commercial-maintenance-contracts/) page covers how that scoping works.

**Forecasting repair spend instead of reacting to it.** Once you know a door's spring type and approximate age, you can estimate roughly when it's entering its wear window — which means a repair can be budgeted for next quarter instead of showing up as an emergency call that disrupts receiving on a Tuesday morning.

None of this requires guessing at numbers. The survey states what's observed; the budget conversation is a separate step the facilities team owns.

sections.heading: When to get one done
sections.body:
A baseline survey makes the most sense in a few specific situations: taking over management of a property with no existing door records, onboarding a new maintenance vendor who needs an honest starting point rather than the previous vendor's notes, preparing a capital budget cycle, or after a portfolio acquisition that added buildings nobody on the team has walked yet.

It's also worth doing simply because it's inexpensive relative to what it prevents. A single walkthrough that catches one spring near end-of-life before it snaps mid-cycle — springs run $175 to $350 to replace on a planned basis — pays for the survey itself several times over, and that's before counting the cost of an unplanned bay-door outage during business hours.

faq.question: What's the difference between a baseline survey and a regular maintenance visit?
faq.answer: A baseline survey happens once, up front, and documents every door's type, age, spring and operator condition, and daily cycle count to create a starting record. A maintenance visit happens on an ongoing schedule afterward, checking each door against that baseline and against what a routine inspection for its door type calls for.

faq.question: How long does a baseline survey take?
faq.answer: It depends on the number of doors on the property — a technician needs enough time at each opening to properly inspect springs, hardware, and operator condition rather than a quick glance. Call (914) 557-6816 with your door count and we can give you a realistic estimate for the walkthrough.

faq.question: Can a baseline survey help justify a capital budget request?
faq.answer: Yes — that's one of its main uses. A written per-door record showing spring type, age, and cycle count turns a general "doors need attention" request into a specific, documented case for which doors need capital spending first and why.

faq.question: Do I need a baseline survey if I already have a maintenance contract?
faq.answer: It's still useful, especially if the existing contract was scoped without one. A baseline shows whether your current maintenance frequency actually matches each door's age and usage, or whether some doors are over-serviced while busier ones are under-checked.
